verses.text: Then Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying,
“Because the leaders took the lead in Israel, because the people offered themselves willingly, be blessed, Yahweh!
“Hear, you kings! Give ear, you princes! I, even I, will sing to Yahweh. I will sing praise to Yahweh, the God of Israel.
“Yahweh, when you went out of Seir, when you marched out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, the sky also dropped. Yes, the clouds dropped water.
The mountains quaked Yahweh’s presence, even Sinai at the presence of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
“In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied. The travelers walked through byways.
The rulers ceased in Israel. They ceased until I, Deborah, arose; Until I arose a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods. Then war was in the gates. Was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart is toward the governors of Israel, who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless Yahweh!
“Speak, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets, and you who walk by the way.

Far from the noise of archers, in the places of drawing water, there they will rehearse Yahweh’s righteous acts, the righteous acts of his rule in Israel. “Then Yahweh’s people went down to the gates.
‘Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, utter a song! Arise, Barak, and lead away your captives, you son of Abinoam.’
“Then a remnant of the nobles and the people came down. Yahweh came down for me against the mighty.
Those whose root is in Amalek came out of Ephraim, after you, Benjamin, among your peoples. Governors come down out of Machir. Those who handle the marshal’s staff came out of Zebulun.
The princes of Issachar were with Deborah. As was Issachar, so was Barak. They rushed into the valley at his feet. By the watercourses of Reuben, there were great resolves of heart.
Why did you sit among the sheepfolds? To hear the whistling for the flocks? At the watercourses of Reuben, there were great searchings of heart.
Gilead lived beyond the Jordan. Why did Dan remain in ships? Asher sat still at the haven of the sea, and lived by his creeks.
Zebulun was a people that jeopardized their lives to the death; Naphtali also, on the high places of the field.
“The kings came and fought, then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo. They took no plunder of silver.
From the sky the stars fought. From their courses, they fought against Sisera.
The river Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. My soul, march on with strength.
Then the horse hoofs stamped because of the prancing, the prancing of their strong ones.
‘Curse Meroz,’ said Yahweh’s angel. ‘Curse bitterly its inhabitants, because they didn’t come to help Yahweh, to help Yahweh against the mighty.’
“Jael shall be blessed above women, the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed shall she be above women in the tent.
He asked for water. She gave him milk. She brought him butter in a lordly dish.
She put her hand to the tent peg, and her right hand to the workmen’s hammer. With the hammer she struck Sisera. She struck through his head. Yes, she pierced and struck through his temples.
At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay. At her feet he bowed, he fell. Where he bowed, there he fell down dead.
“Through the window she looked out, and cried: Sisera’s mother looked through the lattice. ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why do the wheels of his chariots wait?’
Her wise ladies answered her, Yes, she returned answer to herself,

‘Have they not found, have they not divided the plunder? A lady, two ladies to every man; to Sisera a plunder of dyed garments, a plunder of dyed garments embroidered, of dyed garments embroidered on both sides, on the necks of the plunder?’
“So let all your enemies perish, Yahweh, but let those who love him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.”  Then the land had rest forty years.

footnotes.content: When Deborah and Barak sang together after victory, they were doing what God's people have always done: turning their deliverance into praise. Singing can be as much an act of obedience as fighting was—a way of saying, 'We remember, and we're grateful.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the blessing on willing hearts: when the leaders led and the people stepped forward on their own, Deborah called down blessing. God honors the courage of those who volunteer their lives for His purposes—sometimes that matters more than numbers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Deborah spoke as a prophet calling the whole world to witness Israel's God. She knew that what the Lord does in His people tells a story far wider than any single battle. Her witness was blazing and urgent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seir and Edom recall the ancient days when God Himself marched through creation, shaking the earth. Deborah anchors Israel's present victory in the memory of Yahweh's power on display at Sinai—the same God who was shaking mountain and sky.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mountains themselves trembled at His presence. When we sing of God's power, we can rest in the fact that creation itself bears witness to His strength. He is before all things and holds them together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In those dark days under Shamgar and Jael, the roads were empty—too dangerous to travel. Sometimes God works through small deliverers in small moments before He raises up the great ones. Faithfulness in hard seasons plants seeds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Deborah called herself 'a mother in Israel'—not just a judge but a nurturer of her people. She arose when leadership had ceased, when no one else would stand. Sometimes the Lord calls us to be strength for others when the world feels leaderless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Idolatry and emptiness go hand in hand. When Israel chose new gods, they lost not only God's protection but also their own courage—no weapons in hand, no heart to fight. What we worship shapes what we become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Deborah's heart turned toward the commanders who threw themselves into danger willingly. She saw in them the willingness of God's people to answer His call. That voluntary offering of oneself still moves the heart of the faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rich and comfortable—those on white donkeys and cushions—are called to speak. No one stands outside this call to witness. Every station, every comfort, every privilege carries the responsibility to testify to God's righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In places of safety and refreshment—by the wells where people draw water—Israel was meant to rehearse Yahweh's righteous acts. Our gatherings are chances to remind each other of what God has done. Memory is medicine for faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The call to Deborah and Barak is urgent: 'Awake! Arise!' When God calls His people to action, He stirs them as if from sleep. And when they do, captives are freed—those held in bondage walk into light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The nobles and common people together came down to fight because 'Yahweh came down for me.' Deborah knew the source of strength was not in numbers or strategy but in the Lord fighting alongside His people. That changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tribes are named: Amalek's remnant (Ephraim), Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun—each contributing warriors, each answering the call. This is the poetry of a people gathering as one body. The places and tribes are real, rooted, particular.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Issachar's princes stood with Deborah, and Barak rushed into the valley. The watercourses of Reuben heard 'great resolves of heart'—not the noise of doubt or division, but of those resolved. We often underestimate the power of inner resolve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben sat among the sheepfolds, at ease, hearing the whistles of flocks—and 'great searchings of heart' happened there. Even in inaction, conscience wrestles. Some tribes didn't answer. Their hearts searched, but they didn't move. That silence, too, was heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dan remained in ships, Asher sat by his creeks—these were not sloth but choice. Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan. Some were too far, some too settled, some too comfortable by the sea. Geography and circumstance kept them out, or so they reasoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebulun and Naphtali jeopardized their lives to death on the high places. When Deborah sang of them, she was honoring the fierce hearts of those willing to die. That willingness is rare and sacred—it speaks of surrender to something greater.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Taanach, the waters of Megiddo—these places were real ground where real armies fought. No plunder of silver was taken because this was not greed-driven conquest; it was a fight for survival and freedom. The Lord won, and the spoils didn't matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stars themselves fought from their courses—a poetic truth that nature itself moves to God's hand. When we see the cosmos bending toward His purposes, we glimpse a God whose reach is beyond our measure. He commands even the heavens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The river Kishon swept Sisera's army away—ancient river, ancient power. Deborah's soul rose to meet the moment: 'March on with strength.' There is strength in seeing God do what only He can do. The river did what no sword could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sound of horse hooves, the prancing of mighty steeds—and then they were gone, swept away. All that show of strength and prowess; all that confidence in numbers and horses. Before God's hand, it came to nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Curse Meroz'—the city that didn't come to help Yahweh. Neutrality in the face of His work is not silence; it is opposition. To not stand with the Lord when He calls is to stand against Him. There is no middle ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jael, blessed above women—a Kenite woman, not even of Israel, yet used by God to end the tyrant's life. Sometimes the Lord works through unexpected hands. Her name is remembered forever because she stepped forward when the moment came.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sisera asked for water; Jael gave him milk and butter—the warmth of hospitality became the setting for judgment. She didn't rush or make show. She was the image of welcome and care, and in that she fulfilled God's purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jael's hand moved with steady purpose: tent peg, hammer, the head of the oppressor pierced. There is no hesitation in her action, no reluctance. When God calls, even in unexpected ways, His people can move with clarity and strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At her feet he bowed, fell, lay—the mighty commander reduced to a corpse. The repetition underscores the finality. Strength rose, then fell, then stayed fallen. That is how tyranny ends, sometimes not in grand battle but in a tent, at the feet of one faithful woman.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sisera's mother looked through the lattice for her son's chariot, crying out her expectation. The scene shifts suddenly from the tent to a room far away, where a woman waited for a man who would never come. This is the cost of war seen through a mother's eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wise ladies spoke answers to her, and she turned them over in her mind. Even the comfort of companions couldn't ease what was coming—the truth that lay beneath all their rationalizations. Sometimes we know, deep down, what we don't want to face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They spoke of plunder divided: a lady for every man, embroidered garments, spoils. While they imagined the victory feast and the division of captives, their son and commander lay dead in a tent far away. Their confidence was built on sand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in the ending: 'Let those who love Him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.' Deborah's prayer became a promise that remains alive. When we walk with the Lord, we rise not in hidden strength but in the brightness of His favor, visible and unstoppable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
